Arij Soufi est une jeune Montréalaise de: Arij Soufi is a 22-year-old Montrealer who works tirelessly to make it easier for Muslims to be included in Quebec society. She recently received the 2023-2024 Centre Culturel Islamique de Québec Memorial Award. The award was established in 2018 by members of the McGill community in memory of the six men who lost their lives on January 29, 2017, in the attack on the Centre culturel islamique de Québec.
Qui est cette montréalaise et comment pe: Who is this Montrealer, and how does she view Islamophobia in Quebec on the seventh anniversary of the attack on the Québec City mosque? We met with a young woman who wants to break down stereotypes.
Ayant passé toute sa vie dans la métropo: Having spent her whole life in the Montréal area, Arij is a young woman with many ambitions. “I was born in Tunisia, but I did all my schooling in French until university,” she says, opening the conversation.
Si la température extérieure frôle le po: Although the temperature outside is hovering around freezing, the room at McGill University where Arij meets us is pleasant and warm. Students are starting to arrive on campus. They are there to study and review, and the atmosphere is still calm, since it is a Saturday morning.
« Je suis enfin arrivée à ma dernière an: “I’ve finally reached my last year of medical school – finally!” Arij tells us with a smile of relief. “Even though I’m a full-time student, I have other hobbies,” she continues. “I love reading and, recently, I started doing pottery. It’s really nice. I like the feeling of letting loose with my hands without having to worry about precision.”
Arij a un quotidien bien rempli. En plus: Arij’s days are full. In addition to being in the final year of her medical degree, she is co-president of the McGill chapter of the Muslim Medical Association of Canada (MMAC). “When I entered the program five years ago, there was already a Muslim students’ association in coordination with the dentistry program. I remember attending a panel of physicians who explained how they navigated the health care system as Muslims,” she recalls.
« J’étais excitée et motivée à l’idée de: “I was excited and motivated by the idea of getting involved in this association, because for me, it was very important. Unfortunately, the pandemic broke out right then, and most of the members graduated and left the school,” she remembers. Having wanted to get involved to help Muslims thrive in the field of health, she was saddened to see the plan for a Muslim association fall through.
<strong>« On n’obtient jamais tout ce qu: “You never get everything you want when you do advocacy”
« En 2022, un professeur de la faculté a: “In 2022, a professor at the faculty wrote an article in a well-known medical journal in the country. In his piece, he said that the hijab was a tool of oppression and that he didn’t understand why people chose to wear it,” she says. The article was a turning point for Arij. “It really hurt me, especially since he was a teacher I’d had before and whom I appreciated,” she explains.
L’absence d’un groupe de soutien pour fa: The lack of a support group to deal with comments like those made by a teacher left Arij – and other students – feeling powerless. “After that incident, I started, with classmates from the faculty, to see if there was a way to do something. We managed to get meetings with the dean, and we explained to him how hurtful and unacceptable Islamophobic remarks like this professor’s could be, for his colleagues as well as for his students and patients,” she summarizes.
À la suite des démarches entreprises, de: Following these efforts, the professor apologized and retracted his article. While some of the students’ demands were accepted, others proved impossible to achieve – such as his resignation. “You never get everything you want when you do advocacy,” she finally says.
C’est au cours de cet épisode qu’Arij fa: It was during this episode that Arij met several students at the school who shared her values and demands. “At that point, I realized we really had to rebuild the association,” she says.
L’une des principales motivations de la: One of the young citizen’s main motivations was for Muslim students to know that they have a collective, that they have rights, and that there is someone or something there to advocate on their behalf.
À la co-présidence de la MMAC – Chapitre: As co-president of the MMAC – McGill Chapter, Arij Soufi has helped dozens and dozens of students feel they belong. “We organized networking events among Muslim students from several programs at McGill, such as iftars during the month of Ramadan,” she explains. For her, Muslim students needed to feel comfortable “celebrating their faith.”
En plus d’organiser des événements avec: In addition to organizing events with students, she has worked on other projects aimed at the integration and inclusion of Muslims. On the Equity Committee of the McGill student association, she set up a workshop on medical racism. “It came in the wake of the events that followed the tragic death of Joyce Echaquan,” she explains.
Rappelons que Joyce Echaquan est une fem: Joyce Echaquan was an Atikamekw woman who died in 2020 at the Joliette hospital after posting a shocking video on social media in which she was subjected to racist insults and mistreatment by health care staff. The tragedy renewed calls to action to fight systemic racism in the medical field.
« Cet atelier, c’est du contenu qu’on ne: “This workshop is content we aren’t really taught in medicine. Yes, in our courses, we learn that racism is one of the determinants of health; we also learn that we have biases as doctors, but that’s about it. In this workshop, we learn more than that. We learn how not to become complicit in a system that isn’t perfect,” she says passionately.
Dans un projet différent en cours de réa: In a different project under way within the MMAC, “[we] also teach future doctors how to be more culturally sensitive toward people of the Muslim faith. How do you treat a patient who is fasting, for example? Or how do you examine a Muslim patient while protecting her dignity? These are questions we’re working on,” she lists.
« On souhaite aussi offrir un service de:
“We also want to offer a more formal mentorship service,” she says. For the young woman, giving Muslim students people who look like them makes for better representation.

Another of the achievements of the club Arij co-chairs is securing a suitable prayer space for Muslim students.
<strong>« Je veux rester ici, je veux pr: “I want to stay here, I want to practise in Quebec”
Ce qui désespère Arij, c’est la quantité: What dismays Arij is the number of Muslim Quebecers who want to leave the province. “I hear a lot of Muslims say they think Montréal and Quebec are cool, but they don’t see a future here,” she says, discouraged. “The ideal for me would be for young Muslims to be able to imagine a life in Quebec.”
« Pourquoi travailler dans une province: “Why work in a province that hates me? That makes laws to stop me from working in the field I want?” These are statements Arij often hears. “I understand people who have concerns, because those concerns are founded. Yes, I sincerely believe there is Islamophobia in Quebec. But I don’t want young people to think there are no opportunities for them here,” she says, in a more optimistic tone.
« Je veux rester ici, je veux pratiquer: “I want to stay here, I want to practise here. I love this city too much, I want to fight so that Muslims will want to stay here,” she continues.
Arij est consciente qu’il s’agit d’un dé: Arij is aware that this is a challenge for many, and that not everyone has the capacity to take it on. She nevertheless offers a message of hope: “You can’t be afraid to open a path that you’re the first in your community to take. It can be scary for a woman like me, who wears the hijab, to launch into a field made up mostly of white Quebecers, but I’m not afraid to do it!” she exclaims, smiling.
« C’est bien beau de rester dans nos com: “It’s all well and good to stay in our communities, to surround ourselves with people who look like us, but if we really want change, we can’t be afraid to go where people don’t go,” she concludes.
